title: Exchange rates
examples: What is the difference between a fixed and a floating exchange rate?
How does a currency's appreciation affect a country's imports?
Can you explain the effect of depreciation on a country's balance of trade?

explain.say: Today we will look at exchange rates and how they change.

items: They show how much one money buys in another.
This value changes constantly in the market.

explain.say: Some countries use a fixed exchange rate system.

draw.text: Fixed Rate: Pegged to a currency

explain.say: In a fixed system, the central bank actively intervenes in the market.

items: Central bank buys or sells currency
Rate is forced back to the peg

explain.say: A floating exchange rate lets the market determine the value freely.
If your currency appreciates, it means it buys more foreign currency.
If your currency depreciates, it means it buys less foreign currency.

faq.q: What is the difference between appreciation and depreciation?
faq.a: Appreciation means your currency gets stronger, buying more foreign money. Depreciation means your currency gets weaker, buying less foreign money. It is a change in the exchange rate.
asks: What does it mean when a currency weakens?

faq.q: Why do some countries choose a fixed exchange rate?
faq.a: They might choose it to provide stability and reduce uncertainty for international trade. This commitment requires the central bank to intervene regularly.
asks: Is it always better to have a fixed rate?
What is the main goal of keeping a rate fixed?

faq.q: How does currency appreciation affect imports for a country?
faq.a: When your currency appreciates, your goods cost less for foreigners to buy. This generally makes your country's imports more expensive for you.
asks: If my money is stronger, are foreign goods cheaper?
Does a strong currency hurt buying things from abroad?

faq.q: What happens to exports when a country's currency depreciates?
faq.a: A depreciation makes your goods cheaper for buyers in other countries. This can boost your exports and improve the trade balance.
asks: Does a weaker currency help exporters?

faq.q: Is the exchange rate set by governments or by the market?
faq.a: It depends on the system; in a floating system, the market sets it. In a fixed system, the central bank manages it.
asks: Who controls the rate in a floating system?
Can governments control the exchange rate?

facts: A fixed exchange rate requires the central bank to actively buy or sell its own currency.
Currency appreciation means that one unit of local currency can buy more units of foreign currency.
Currency depreciation makes a country's exports cheaper for international buyers.
In a floating system, supply and demand in the foreign exchange market determine the rate.

quiz.say: If the US dollar appreciates against the euro, what happens to a US tourist buying a car in Germany?

options.show: The car becomes cheaper for the US tourist.
options.say: The car becomes cheaper for the US tourist.

options.show: The car becomes more expensive for the US tourist.
options.say: The car becomes more expensive for the US tourist.

options.show: The price of the car remains exactly the same.
options.say: The price of the car remains exactly the same.

options.show: The German seller must lower their price.
options.say: The German seller must lower their price.

quiz.why: Appreciation means the dollar buys more euros, making the foreign good less expensive for the US buyer.

wrong.2: Exchange rates constantly change the cost of foreign goods.
wrong.3: The exchange rate change affects the buyer's cost, not the seller's local price.

quiz.say: A country switches to a floating exchange rate system. What is the main implication?

options.show: The market forces will determine the new currency value.
options.say: The market forces will determine the new currency value.

options.show: The central bank must immediately buy all foreign currency.
options.say: The central bank must immediately buy all foreign currency.

options.show: All trade must stop until a new rate is set.
options.say: All trade must stop until a new rate is set.

options.show: The government must set a new fixed peg immediately.
options.say: The government must set a new fixed peg immediately.

quiz.why: Floating rates rely on the natural forces of supply and demand, not central bank orders.

wrong.1: Buying currency is an action taken to prevent a float, not what happens when switching to it.
wrong.2: Trade continues; the rate simply adjusts based on market activity.
wrong.3: Switching to floating means giving up the ability to set a fixed peg.

quiz.say: If the local currency depreciates, how does this affect the cost of imported electronics for local consumers?

options.show: The imported electronics become more expensive.
options.say: The imported electronics become more expensive.

options.show: The electronics become cheaper because demand increases.
options.say: The electronics become cheaper because demand increases.

options.show: The price will stay the same because local shops absorb the change.
options.say: The price will stay the same because local shops absorb the change.

options.show: The rate will automatically adjust back to the old level.
options.say: The rate will automatically adjust back to the old level.

quiz.why: A weaker local currency means you need more of your money to buy the same amount of foreign currency needed for the electronics.

wrong.1: While high demand exists, the cost is determined by the exchange rate, not just demand.
wrong.2: Local shops usually pass on the increased cost from foreign suppliers.
wrong.3: Depreciation is a market movement, and the rate will settle at a new, lower value.
